local_facts.claim: Colorado has no statewide mold-remediation licensing or registration program. In 2025, HB25-1202 proposed a Mold Awareness and Registration Act that would have required registration for mold assessment and remediation providers, but the bill was lost.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A homeowner cannot rely on a state mold license lookup. The written scope, training or third-party certifications, containment plan, moisture-source plan, and a clear boundary between cleaning and removal are the practical ways to compare proposed work.
local_facts.title: There is no Colorado mold license to look up

local_facts.claim: Colorado Springs has a 1991–2020 annual precipitation normal of 15.91 inches, according to the National Weather Service.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Low outdoor humidity can make residents dismiss a musty room. At a property with mold, the inspection should follow a localized indoor water source such as a slow plumbing leak, roof entry, appliance connection, or damp below-grade area rather than blaming the regional climate.
local_facts.title: Dry outdoor air can hide a wet wall cavity

local_facts.claim: Colorado Springs planning data lists a median year of construction of 1986. Its 2020–2024 consolidated plan says 42% of owner-occupied and 47% of renter-occupied homes were built before 1980, totaling more than 77,000 homes.
local_facts.why_it_matters: The housing stock spans many renovation histories, insulation conditions, roof repairs, and concealed plumbing routes. An attic, wall, or crawl-space scope should be based on the actual water path and accessible materials rather than a one-size assumption about the building.
local_facts.title: The city’s housing stock has many hidden water paths
